title: IRQ and preemption probe playbook for latency spikes
summary: Hands-on playbook for diagnosing tail-latency spikes caused by IRQ/preemption interactions and kernel-user boundary stalls. Includes probe scripts, collection commands, artifact expectations, interpretation heuristics, and quick mitigations.
body:
Purpose:
This doc is a lightweight runbook for engineers triaging persistent tail-latency spikes where CPU preemption, interrupt storms, or kernel->user boundary latencies (including driver / IRQ handling) are suspected. It focuses on practical tooling and scripts we use in perf CI and on-host investigations and how to interpret outputs to quickly decide mitigation vs. deeper follow-up.

When to run this playbook:
- Intermittent but repeatable 95th/99th token latency regressions
- Sudden GPU stalls where application threads report long wakelatency
- Symptoms in telemetry: sudden increase in sched_wakeup/sched_switch time, high softirq/irq cycles, or long syscalls in span traces

Quick checklist (run first):
1) Confirm spike window in traces/console (route + model + region).
2) Grab correlating host metrics (top, iostat, vmstat, dstat).
3) If reproducible, schedule a collection window (5–120s depending on workload) on an affected instance.

Required pieces (local or CI runner):
- perf (Linux kernel perf tools) >= 5.10
- FlameGraph scripts (Brendangregg/FlameGraph) in PATH
- bpftrace (optional, for aggregated histograms)
- trace-cmd / kernelshark (optional)
- small helper scripts in runtime/tools/irq-probes (see linked GitHub)

Collection recipes (low-noise first):
A) Lightweight wallclock flame (preferred for short windows)
- sudo perf record -F 99 -g --call-graph dwarf -a -- sleep 30
- sudo perf script > perf.folded
- stackcollapse-perf.pl perf.script > perf.folded (if using older tools)
- flamegraph.pl perf.folded > flame.svg
Notes: -F sets sample frequency; reduce to 49 for very noisy systems. Use --call-graph dwarf for accurate user+kernel stacks.

B) IRQ/softirq focused capture
- sudo perf record -e irq:irq_handler_entry -e irq:irq_handler_exit -e softirq:softirq_entry -e softirq:softirq_exit -g -a -- sleep 30
- perf script | awk '/irq/ || /softirq/ {print}' > irq.events.txt
- Parse /proc/interrupts before/after collection: cat /proc/interrupts > interrupts.before
  (run again after collection)

C) bpftrace aggregated latency histograms (fast summary)
- sudo bpftrace -e 'kprobe:sched_wakeup { @[comm] = hist((nsecs - kstack())) }' --duration 20s
(we provide curated bpftrace scripts in runtime/tools/irq-probes/ to avoid noisy raw probes)

D) GPU-driver boundary stalls (NVIDIA example)
- Collect dmesg and nvidia-smi dmon during window
- sudo perf record -e 'syscalls:sys_enter_*' -e 'syscalls:sys_exit_*' -g -a -- sleep 20
- Look for long entries in perf script that show user->kernel->user transitions with driver frames between.

Expected artifacts to upload to ticket/PR:
- perf.data (compressed), perf.script (text), perf.folded, flame.svg
- irq.events.txt, interrupts.before, interrupts.after
- bpftrace.log or histogram.png (if used)
- dmesg snippets (filtered), kernel version (uname -a), cpu topology output (lscpu)

Interpretation guide (common patterns):
1) Flame spanning kernel/user boundary with driver frames in middle -> likely driver IRQ handler or ioctl holding a spinlock. Mitigation: escalate to driver team, or try isolating thread to different CPU, or disable problematic IRQ coalescing.
2) Softirq hot path dominates (top of flame is ksoftirqd) -> look at NIC RX load, irq affinity, RPS/RFS settings. Quick mitigation: adjust irq affinity, enable XPS/RPS, ensure no IRQ sharing for high-throughput queues.
3) Frequent preemptions seen in stacks with scheduler frames -> short CPU bursts preempting hot threads (e.g., cron jobs or container GC). Use cgroup cpu controller to limit background tasks or set CPU isolcpus for inference threads.
4) Sparse but very long syscall stacks (blocked in driver) -> kernel bug or contention in device driver; collect stack traces repeatedly to confirm.

Guided triage flow:
- Step 0: Confirm trace spans the same time range as spike. Attach trace IDs to artifacts.
- Step 1: Look for obvious system-wide events (OOM, kernel warnings in dmesg).
- Step 2: Open flame.svg; color by user vs kernel (FlameGraph has options). If kernel frames appear as narrow stacks but with high weight, suspect IRQ.
- Step 3: Correlate /proc/interrupts to identify which vector increased during the window. Map IRQ to device: sudo cat /proc/irq/<n>/smp_affinity and check /sys/bus/pci/devices/*/irq.
- Step 4: If NIC-related, check ethtool -S, RPS/XPS, and qdisc misconfiguration.
- Step 5: If GPU-related, look at nvidia-smi -q and kernel log for GPU resets; capture vendor driver frames for escalation.

Automated checks to add to perf CI (ideas):
- Scheduled nightly capture of 10s flame under synthetic steady-state workload; run lightweight script to ensure softirq/irq % doesn’t spike > 3% of CPU time.
- A small regression test that runs a short bpftrace histogram and fails if sched_wakeup histogram tail shifts > 2x baseline.

Common quick mitigations (orders of magnitude):
- Rebalance irq affinity to spread high-frequency interrupts across sockets (low cost).
- Enable interrupt coalescing on NICs if latency budget allows (medium cost: possible throughput tradeoff).
- Pin inference worker threads to isolated CPUs and set SCHED_FIFO for critical threads (medium/high cost: scheduling risk).
- Upgrade vendor driver or kernel if a known bug (high cost/coordination).

Owner & escalation:
- Primary: eng-serving-runtime on-call (include perf artifacts).
- If driver/NIC suspected: escalate to infra-networking or vendor support with perf files and /proc/interrupts.
- For GPU driver stalls: escalate to infra-gpu and include vendor trace and nvcrash logs.

Follow-ups & tickets to open when confirmed:
- INFRA-NIC-<date>: irq affinity policy change (include before/after perf)
- RUNTIME-BUG-XXXX: protect KV cache hot path from preemption if long syscalls observed
- DRIVER-ESCALATE-YYYY: vendor driver stack dump + kernel debug logs

Housekeeping (what to upload to a ticket):
- One-line reproduction: exact command used and duration
- Host snapshot: uname -a, lscpu, /proc/interrupts (before/after), dmesg excerpt
- Perf artifacts and a single annotated flame.svg with problem frames highlighted (we annotate using inkscape or a simple SVG editor)

Appendix: useful commands (copy/paste)
- Capture perf: sudo perf record -F 99 -g -a -- sleep 30
- Convert to script: sudo perf script > perf.script
- Generate folded (FlameGraph toolkit): ./stackcollapse-perf.pl perf.script > perf.folded
- Generate flame: ./flamegraph.pl perf.folded > flame.svg
- IRQ peek: cat /proc/interrupts | egrep -i "eth|gpu|nvidia|mlx|ioat|nvme"
- Map IRQ -> device: for i in $(cat /proc/interrupts | awk '/eth|mlx|nvme|nvidia/ {print $1}' | sed 's/://'); do ls -l /proc/irq/$i; done

Notes & caveats:
- perf on cloud images sometimes has symbol issues; ensure debug symbols or use addr2line against our runtime binary on the same build.
- Flamegraphs collapse many frames; when in doubt, use perf script and inspect raw callstacks.
- bpftrace probes can perturb timing for very latency-sensitive workloads; prefer short duration and gather multiple runs.

Owner contact and history:
- Author: Ava Moreno (eng-serving-runtime)
- Maintainers: Kai Zhang (profiling infra), Leah Patel (kernel tools), Jonas Müller (gpu infra)
- Origin: distilled from multiple on-call incidents in 2024–2025, adapted into a perf CI checklist in Q1 2025.

If you follow this playbook and still can't find the root cause, attach artifacts and open a ticket with the triage checklist filled out. Provide at least two independent collection windows separated by a few minutes if the issue is intermittent.
